claim: KIF21B protein is expressed in Jurkat T lymphocyte cells.
source: We confirmed KIF21B protein expression in these cells by Western blotting (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Confirmed by Western blot analysis showing KIF21B protein bands in control Jurkat cells.

claim: Two KIF21B knockout clones (#1 and #2) were generated using CRISPR/Cas9 technology and showed loss of KIF21B expression.
source: Using CRISPR/Cas9 technology we generated KIF21B knockout cells and selected two clones (#1 and #2) that were analyzed further.
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 1C shows absence of KIF21B protein in knockout clones.

claim: KIF21B-GFP expression in rescue cell lines mildly exceeded endogenous KIF21B levels.
source: KIF21B expression was lost in both knockout lines, whereas KIF21B-GFP expression mildly exceeded endogenous KIF21B.
evidence: Western blot comparison of KIF21B band intensity between control and rescue lines in Figure 1C.

claim: KIF21B knockout does not affect CD3ε expression in Jurkat T cells.
source: In addition, we established that these Jurkat T cell lines were responsive to stimulus by first confirming the presence of CD3ε, a subunit of the T cell receptor (TCR) (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Western blot shows CD3ε bands in all cell lines including knockouts.

claim: KIF21B knockout cells respond similarly to control cells in IL-2 upregulation after PMA and ionomycin stimulation.
source: This stimulation regime upregulates Interleukin-2 (IL-2) mRNA expression, a hallmark of T cell activation, and we found that our knockout cell lines responded similarly to control cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: qRT-PCR data showing comparable IL-2 expression levels across control and knockout lines.

claim: KIF21B-KO cells form 28.4% (KO #1) and 27.3% (KO #2) smaller immunological synapses compared to control cells.
source: We measured synapse size and noticed that KIF21B-KO cell lines formed 28.4% (KO #1) and 27.3% (KO #2) smaller synapses compared to control cells and that this phenotype could be partially rescued by re-expression of KIF21B-GFP (Figure 1E).
evidence: Quantification of synapse surface area from phalloidin-stained cells shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The reduction in immunological synapse size in KIF21B-KO cells is not due to smaller overall cell size.
source: The reduction in the size of immunological synapses in KIF21B-KO cells was not due to smaller overall size of these cells, as their volume was the same as that of control cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: Cell volume measurements from F-actin staining showing no significant difference between control and KO cells.

claim: Synapse formation is slower in KIF21B-KO cells compared to control cells.
source: Live-cell imaging using Differential Interference Contrast (DIC) microscopy showed that synapse formation was slower in KIF21B-KO cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–G).
evidence: DIC microscopy time-lapse data showing increased spreading time in KO cells.

claim: In control cells, the centrosome was located in the plane of the synapse in 76% of cells, whereas in KIF21B-KO cells this occurred in only 45.5% (KO #1) and 43.6% (KO #2) of cells.
source: In this experiment, the centrosome was located in the plane of the synapse in the majority of control (76%) and KIF21B-GFP-expressing cells (74.3% and 63.3%), whereas this was the case only in 45.5% (KO #1) and 43.6% (KO #2) of KIF21B-KO cells (Figure 1G).
evidence: TIRF microscopy quantification of MT organization showing radial vs disorganized patterns.

claim: KIF21B knockout does not affect lysosome clustering around the centrosome after T cell activation.
source: In contrast, after activation on anti-CD3-coated coverslips, both control and knockout cells showed lysosome clustering, indicating that KIF21B knockout does not affect the minus-end-directed transport of lysosomes (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: Immunostaining showing Lamtor4-positive lysosome clusters in both control and KO cells.

claim: Only 52.4% of KIF21B-KO #1 and 50.4% of KIF21B-KO #2 cells contained a polarized lysosome cluster compared to 71% of control cells.
source: We then analyzed the position of the lysosome cluster relative to the coverslip using z-projections of these cells and found that only 52.4% KIF21B-KO #1% and 50.4% KIF21B-KO #2 cells contained a polarized lysosome cluster compared to 71% of control cells (Figure 1I,J).
evidence: 3D analysis of Lamtor4 cluster distance from coverslip showing reduced polarization in KO cells.

claim: KIF21B-KO cells have an increased proportion of non-radially oriented microtubules organized into peripheral MT bundles at the immunological synapse.
source: This analysis showed that KIF21B-KO cells have an increased proportion of non-radially oriented MTs, which are organized into peripheral MT bundles at the immunological synapse (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: STED microscopy images analyzed with custom ImageJ plugin showing increased non-radial MT intensity in KO cells.

claim: KIF21B-KO cells contain fewer microtubules nucleated from the centrosome, reduced by 21.7% in KO #1 and 19% in KO #2.
source: We found that MT number was slightly reduced in KIF21B-KO cells, by 21.7% in KO #1% and 19% in KO #2 (Figure 2F).
evidence: Expansion microscopy quantification of MTs crossing a spherical shell around the centrosome.

claim: Microtubules in KIF21B-KO cells are on average longer than those in control cells.
source: We found that KIF21B-KO cells contain fewer MTs but they are on average longer than those in control cells (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: Expansion microscopy analysis estimating MT length from fluorescence intensity measurements.

claim: The overall microtubule mass is higher in KIF21B-KO cells compared to control cells.
source: Since the overall MT mass is higher in KIF21B-KO cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B), the concentration of free tubulin in these cells might be lower; this would affect MT nucleation at the centrosome, causing a reduction in MT number.
evidence: Expansion microscopy data showing total estimated MT length per cell is higher in KO cells.

claim: KIF21B-GFP does not show cortical accumulation in T cells but is diffusely distributed in the cytoplasm or associated with microtubules.
source: Likewise, KIF21B-GFP did not show any obvious cortical accumulation in T cells but was rather diffusely distributed in the cytoplasm or associated to MTs on which it moved processively (Figure 3A, Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: Live-cell imaging showing KIF21B-GFP localization and movement patterns.

claim: The average velocity of KIF21B-GFP puncta in T cells is 0.77 ± 0.14 µm/s.
source: The average velocity of KIF21B-GFP puncta was 0.77 ± 0.14 µm/s (mean ± SD) (Figure 3A,B), which is 1.2 and almost four times faster compared to velocities measured for the full-length motor in COS-7 cells and hippocampal neurons, respectively (Ghiretti et al., 2016; van Riel et al., 2017).
evidence: Kymograph analysis of KIF21B-GFP tracks in live T cells.

claim: Most motile KIF21B-GFP puncta in Jurkat cells correspond to single kinesin dimers.
source: Most of the motile KIF21B-GFP puncta in Jurkat cells thus likely corresponded to single kinesin dimers, which did not form any clear accumulations.
evidence: Single-molecule fluorescence intensity analysis comparing KIF21B-GFP to monomeric GFP showing ~2x intensity after distance correction.

claim: 56.7% of KIF21B-GFP molecules transition to a paused state upon reaching a microtubule plus end.
source: Most of KIF21B-GFP molecules (56.7%) transitioned to a paused state upon reaching the plus end; some motors (29.5%) dissociated from the MT and in a few cases KIF21B tracked the MT tip and then either transitioned to a paused state (9.8%) or dissociated from the MT (4%) (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: Live-cell imaging quantification of KIF21B-GFP behavior at EB3-mCherry-labeled MT plus ends.

claim: When KIF21B-GFP pauses at a microtubule plus end, 55.7% of events result in the MT switching to depolymerization.
source: A pausing KIF21B-GFP motor typically did affect MT plus-end growth, and the events where a MT first paused and ultimately switched to depolymerization were most frequent (55.7%).
evidence: Quantification of MT plus-end fates when KIF21B-GFP pauses at the tip.

claim: KIF21B-GFP motors pause for an average of 3.0 ± 2.7 s at microtubule plus ends.
source: On average, KIF21B-GFP motors were paused for 3.0 ± 2.7 s (mean ± SD) (Figure 3I), whereas MT plus-end pause durations measured with EB3-mCherry were somewhat longer, 4.2 ± 4.4 s (mean ± SD) (Figure 3I).
evidence: Quantification of pause duration from live-cell imaging of KIF21B-GFP and EB3-mCherry.

claim: Microtubule growth rate is increased by 18% in KIF21B-KO #1 and 15% in KIF21B-KO #2 compared to control Jurkat cells.
source: We found that the MT growth rate was on average increased by 18% (KO #1) and 15% (KO #2) compared to control Jurkat cells (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: EB3-GFP live imaging showing increased MT growth rates in KO cells.

claim: Microtubule catastrophe rate is decreased in KIF21B knockout cells.
source: Furthermore, we observed a decrease in MT catastrophe rate in KIF21B knockout cells (Figure 4C), which fits well with previous studies in neurons (Ghiretti et al., 2016; Muhia et al., 2016).
evidence: EB3-GFP imaging quantification showing reduced catastrophe frequency in KO cells.

claim: In control cells, 44.2% of microtubules pause and 40.9% buckle when reaching the cell periphery.
source: In control cells, a small minority (9.8%) of MTs underwent a catastrophe or continued to grow by sliding along the cell cortex (Figure 4D,E). However, most MTs paused in this region (44.2%) or continued their growth and this led to MT buckling, because the MT plus end remained stationary, whereas the increasingly long MT shaft was pushed backwards and formed a loop (40.9%) (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: Live-cell imaging of β-tubulin-GFP showing MT plus-end fates at the cell periphery.

claim: In KIF21B-KO cells, microtubules display less pausing at the cell periphery, whereas buckling becomes more frequent.
source: In KIF21B-KO cells, MTs displayed less pausing at the cell periphery, whereas buckling became more frequent (Figure 4E).
evidence: Quantification of MT plus-end fates showing increased buckling and decreased pausing in KO cells.

claim: Microtubule pause durations in control cells (8.3 ± 5.6 s) are significantly longer than in KIF21B-KO cells (4.1 ± 2.2 s for KO #1 and 4.3 ± 2.4 s for KO #2).
source: A closer examination of MT pauses revealed that these events in control cells were significantly more long-lived: 8.3 ± 5.6 s (mean ± SD) compared to those in KIF21B-KO cells: 4.1 ± 2.2 s (KO #1, mean ± SD) and 4.3 ± 2.4 s (KO #2, mean ± SD) (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Quantification of pause duration from β-tubulin-GFP imaging at the cell periphery.

claim: Treatment with 0.5 nM vinblastine preserves the microtubule network and prevents formation of circular MT bundles at the cell periphery in KIF21B-KO cells.
source: Indeed, at a low (0.5 nM) vinblastine concentration, MT network was preserved and was similar to that in control cells but different from KIF21B-KO cells, as no circular MT bundles were present at the cell periphery (compare Figure 4—figure supplement 1B to Figure 2A).
evidence: STED microscopy images showing MT organization in vinblastine-treated KO cells.

claim: Treatment with 0.5 nM vinblastine reduces microtubule growth rates in KIF21B-KO cells to approximately the level seen in control cells.
source: In vinblastine-treated KIF21B-KO cells, MT growth events visualized with EB3-GFP were less continuous, and the growth rates were reduced approximately to the level seen in control Jurkat cells (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: EB3-GFP imaging showing reduced growth rates in vinblastine-treated KO cells.

claim: Treatment with 0.5 nM vinblastine rescues centrosome polarization defects in KIF21B-KO cells.
source: We scored polarization events as successful when the centrosome was located within 2 µm from the coverslip and found that most control cells (87.2%) were polarized, contrary to knockout cells (36.7% and 42.9%) (Figure 4H). This phenotype could be partially rescued by reexpressing KIF21B-GFP in these cells (58.9% and 51.7%), and an even slightly better rescue was observed after applying 0.5 nM vinblastine to both KIF21B-KO cell lines (65.4% and 66.9%) (Figure 4H,I).
evidence: 3D analysis of CEP135 distance from coverslip showing improved polarization with vinblastine treatment.

claim: Cell polarization defects caused by the absence of KIF21B are due to its effect on microtubule dynamics rather than perturbation of transport or signaling processes.
source: This indicates that cell polarization defects caused by the absence of KIF21B are due to its effect on MT dynamics rather than potential perturbation of transport or signaling processes.
evidence: Rescue of polarization defects by vinblastine, which affects MT dynamics but not KIF21B-dependent transport or signaling.

claim: A small number of KIF21B molecules (4-10 motors) is sufficient to restrict microtubule length in computational simulations.
source: In our simulations, a small number of KIF21B motors was sufficient to prevent the overgrowth of the MT network.
evidence: Cytosim modeling showing mean MT length decreases with increasing number of KIF21B motors (Figure 5F).

claim: In simulations, cells with longer microtubules need more time on average to polarize.
source: In both the non-pausing as well as in the KIF21B-pausing model, the cells with longer MTs needed more time on average to polarize (Figures 5D,F and 6C,D).
evidence: Cytosim simulation results showing correlation between MT length and polarization time.

claim: Some simulated KIF21B-KO-like cells without KIF21B did not polarize within 800 s of simulation time.
source: Some KIF21B-KO-like cells without KIF21B and some cells with a fixed catastrophe rate smaller than 0.03 s−1 did not polarize at the end of the simulation (800 s modeled time that we simulated after the MT network reached steady state).
evidence: Cytosim simulation data showing unpolarized cells at end of simulation time (Figure 6C,D).

claim: Dynein forces are more balanced in simulations with low KIF21B numbers and impaired polarization than in simulations with high KIF21B numbers and rapid polarization.
source: The resulting data revealed that dynein forces were more balanced in the simulations with low KIF21B numbers and impaired polarization than in the simulations where the number of KIF21B molecules was high and polarization occurred rapidly.
evidence: Cytosim simulation quantification of force imbalance showing greater balance with fewer KIF21B motors (Figure 6F).

claim: With increasing number of KIF21B molecules in simulations, the mean number of microtubules bound to dynein decreases while the difference between left and right sides increases.
source: This analysis indicated that with increasing number of KIF21B molecules, the mean number of MTs bound on the left or on right decreases, while the difference between the two fractions averaged over time increases.
evidence: Cytosim simulation quantification of MT binding to dynein showing reduced total binding and increased asymmetry with more KIF21B (Figure 6G).

claim: KIF21B restricts microtubule length by inducing microtubule pausing typically followed by catastrophe.
source: KIF21B restricts microtubule length by inducing microtubule pausing typically followed by catastrophe.
evidence: Live-cell imaging showing KIF21B-GFP induces MT pausing and catastrophe at plus ends.

claim: Catastrophe induction with vinblastine prevented microtubule overgrowth and was sufficient to rescue centrosome polarization in KIF21B-knockout cells.
source: Catastrophe induction with vinblastine prevented microtubule overgrowth and was sufficient to rescue centrosome polarization in KIF21B-knockout cells.
evidence: Experimental data showing vinblastine treatment restores MT length and centrosome polarization in KO cells.

claim: Biophysical simulations showed that a relatively small number of KIF21B molecules can restrict microtubule length and promote an imbalance of dynein-mediated pulling forces.
source: Biophysical simulations showed that a relatively small number of KIF21B molecules can restrict mirotubule length and promote an imbalance of dynein-mediated pulling forces that allows the centrosome to translocate past the nucleus.
evidence: Cytosim modeling results showing MT length restriction and force imbalance with small numbers of KIF21B motors.

claim: Proper control of microtubule length is important for allowing rapid remodeling of the cytoskeleton and efficient T cell polarization.
source: We conclude that proper control of microtubule length is important for allowing rapid remodeling of the cytoskeleton and efficient T cell polarization.
evidence: Combined experimental and computational evidence showing MT length affects polarization efficiency.

claim: KIF21B is linked to autoimmune disorders.
source: Here, we show that the knockout of KIF21B, a kinesin-4 linked to autoimmune disorders, causes microtubule overgrowth and perturbs centrosome translocation.
evidence: Citation of multiple studies linking KIF21B gene to immune-related disorders.

claim: Several studies have linked the KIF21B gene to neurodevelopmental and immune-related disorders, including multiple sclerosis and inflammatory conditions.
source: Several studies have linked the KIF21B gene to neurodevelopmental and immune-related disorders, including multiple sclerosis and inflammatory conditions such as Crohn's disease and ankylosing spondylitis (Anderson et al., 2009; Asselin et al., 2020; Barrett et al., 2008; Garcia-Etxebarria et al., 2016; Goris et al., 2010; International Multiple Sclerosis Genetics Consortium (IMSGC), 2010; Kannan et al., 2017; Kreft et al., 2014; Li et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2013b; Robinson et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: Multiple cited studies establishing genetic associations between KIF21B and various disorders.

claim: Kif21b knockout mice are viable but show behavioral deficits and defects in synaptic transmission.
source: Kif21b knock out mice are viable but show behavioral deficits and defects in synaptic transmission (Ghiretti et al., 2016; Gromova et al., 2018; Morikawa et al., 2018; Muhia et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited studies describing phenotypes of Kif21b knockout mice.

claim: KIF21B has been reported to be a processive kinesin involved in neuronal transport.
source: At the cellular level, KIF21B has been reported to be a processive kinesin involved in neuronal transport (Ghiretti et al., 2016; Gromova et al., 2018; Labonté et al., 2014) and Rac1 inactivation (Morikawa et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited studies reporting KIF21B functions in neurons.

claim: KIF21B acts as a microtubule growth regulator both in vitro and in cells.
source: Furthermore, similar to all other kinesin-4 family members, KIF21B acts as a MT growth regulator both in vitro and in cells (Ghiretti et al., 2016; Muhia et al., 2016; van Riel et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited studies demonstrating KIF21B's role in regulating MT growth.

claim: One study reported that KIF21B acts as a positive regulator of MT dynamicity by increasing MT growth rate and catastrophe frequency at relatively high concentrations (50-300 nM).
source: However, the activity of this kinesin is a matter of controversy, because one study reported that it acts as a positive regulator of MT dynamicity by increasing MT growth rate and catastrophe frequency; in these assays, KIF21B was present at relatively high concentrations (50–300 nM) and was mainly observed to bind to depolymerizing MT ends and lattices (Ghiretti et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited study by Ghiretti et al. reporting specific KIF21B activities at high concentrations.

claim: Previous work showed that KIF21B walks to MT plus ends where it slows down MT growth and potently induces MT pausing at low nanomolar concentrations.
source: In contrast, our own work showed that KIF21B walks to MT plus ends where it slows down MT growth and potently induces MT pausing already at low nanomolar concentrations, with only one or two KIF21B molecules being sufficient to block elongation of a MT plus end (van Riel et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited previous work by the authors showing KIF21B activity at low concentrations.

claim: When a T cell encounters an antigen-presenting cell, it translocates its centrosome and associated MTs toward the APC-contact side.
source: For example, when a T cell encounters an antigen-presenting cell (APC), it translocates its centrosome and associated MTs toward the APC-contact side (Geiger et al., 1982; Kupfer et al., 1983; Stinchcombe et al., 2006; Yi et al., 2013) and forms an immunological synapse (reviewed in Dustin et al., 2010), a highly specialized compartment encircled by an actin-rich ring.
evidence: Cited studies describing centrosome translocation in T cells during synapse formation.

claim: The process of centrosome repositioning in T cells takes only a few minutes.
source: The process of centrosome repositioning takes only a few minutes and is driven by membrane-associated dynein that pulls MTs with the attached centrosome toward the synapse (Combs et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2013a; Martín-Cófreces et al., 2008; Nath et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited studies describing the timescale and mechanism of centrosome repositioning.

claim: Centrosome repositioning in T cells is driven by membrane-associated dynein that pulls microtubules with the attached centrosome toward the synapse.
source: The process of centrosome repositioning takes only a few minutes and is driven by membrane-associated dynein that pulls MTs with the attached centrosome toward the synapse (Combs et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2013a; Martín-Cófreces et al., 2008; Nath et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited studies establishing dynein as the force generator for centrosome movement.

claim: MT-associated protein MAP4 is required for centrosome translocation in T cells.
source: Among them, MT-associated protein MAP4 was shown to be required for centrosome translocation (Bustos-Morán et al., 2017), potentially due to its ability to regulate dynein (Samora et al., 2011; Semenova et al., 2014; Seo et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited studies showing MAP4's role in centrosome translocation and dynein regulation.

claim: Both acetylation and detyrosination of MTs and a complex of casein kinase Iδ with EB1 are important for efficient centrosome polarization in T cells.
source: In addition, both acetylation and detyrosination of MTs and a complex of casein kinase Iδ with EB1 were suggested to be important for efficient centrosome polarization (Andrés-Delgado et al., 2012; Serrador et al., 2004; Zyss et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited studies suggesting roles for MT modifications and EB1 complex in polarization.

claim: Knockout of stathmin/OP18 in mouse cytotoxic T cells showed decreased centrosome polarization efficiency.
source: Finally, a study describing the knockout of stathmin/OP18, a MT-destabilizing protein, in mouse cytotoxic T cells showed decreased centrosome polarization efficiency (Filbert et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited study showing effect of stathmin knockout on T cell polarization.

claim: Kinesin-4 family members are well known for their ability to limit MT growth in a variety of cellular processes.
source: Kinesin-4 family members are well known for their ability to limit MT growth in a variety of cellular processes (Bieling et al., 2010; Bringmann et al., 2004; He et al., 2014; Yue et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited studies establishing kinesin-4 family function in limiting MT growth.

claim: KIF21A and KIF21B consist of an N-terminal motor domain, several coiled-coil regions and a C-terminal WD40 domain.
source: Among them are two closely related motors KIF21A and KIF21B, which consist of an N-terminal motor domain, several coiled-coil regions and a C-terminal WD40 domain (Marszalek et al., 1999).
evidence: Cited study describing the domain structure of KIF21A and KIF21B.

claim: Point mutations in KIF21A that impair its auto-inhibition lead to congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles type 1 (CFEOM1).
source: KIF21A is expressed in many tissues; it is well studied because point mutations impairing its auto-inhibition lead to congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles type 1 (CFEOM1), a neurodevelopmental disorder that affects eye movement (Bianchi et al., 2016; Cheng et al., 2014; Traboulsi and Engle, 2004; van der Vaart et al., 2013; Yamada et al., 2003).
evidence: Cited studies linking KIF21A mutations to CFEOM1 disease.

claim: In vitro, KIF21A slows down MT growth and suppresses catastrophes.
source: In vitro, KIF21A slows down MT growth and suppresses catastrophes, whereas in cells it prevents overgrowth of MTs at the cell cortex (van der Vaart et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited study describing KIF21A's effects on MT dynamics in vitro and in cells.

claim: KIF21B is expressed in brain, eyes, and spleen.
source: KIF21B is expressed in brain, eyes, and spleen (Marszalek et al., 1999).
evidence: Cited study reporting tissue expression pattern of KIF21B.

claim: KIF21B does not possess the KANK-binding region required for association with cortical MT stabilizing complexes.
source: Structural studies have elucidated the binding interface of this interaction, and it is clear that KIF21B does not possess the KANK-binding region required for association with the CMSC (Guo et al., 2018; Pan et al., 2018; Weng et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited structural studies showing KIF21B lacks KANK-binding region.

claim: The velocity of KIF21B-GFP in T cells is 1.2 times faster than in COS-7 cells and almost four times faster than in hippocampal neurons.
source: The average velocity of KIF21B-GFP puncta was 0.77 ± 0.14 µm/s (mean ± SD) (Figure 3A,B), which is 1.2 and almost four times faster compared to velocities measured for the full-length motor in COS-7 cells and hippocampal neurons, respectively (Ghiretti et al., 2016; van Riel et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparison of measured velocities with cited studies in other cell types.

claim: Overexpression of KIF21B-GFP in COS-7 cells reduced MT growth rates by approximately 1.5-fold.
source: These observations were in line with previous work showing that overexpression of KIF21B-GFP in COS-7 cells, which do not have endogenous KIF21B, reduced MT growth rates by ~1.5-fold (van Riel et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited previous work showing KIF21B's effect on MT growth in COS-7 cells.

claim: Transient KIF21B depletion in neurons increased MT growth rate.
source: These data are also consistent with the observation of increased MT growth rate after transient KIF21B depletion in neurons (Ghiretti et al., 2016), but contradict the analysis of MT growth speed in Kif21b knockout neurons (Muhia et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited studies showing conflicting results on KIF21B's effect on MT growth in neurons.

claim: A low dose of vinblastine mildly perturbs MT growth and promotes catastrophes but does not induce MT depolymerization.
source: Our previous work has shown that a low dose of vinblastine mildly perturbs growth and promotes catastrophes but does not induce MT depolymerization (Bouchet et al., 2016; Mohan et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited previous work characterizing low-dose vinblastine effects on MTs.

claim: A previous computational model suggested that in a T cell with a static overgrown MT network the centrosome can be trapped behind the nucleus.
source: However, a previous computational model in three dimensions suggested that in a T cell with a static overgrown MT network the centrosome can be trapped behind the nucleus (Kim and Maly, 2009), and in our ExM data we do observe KIF21B-KO cells with an apically located centrosome and symmetric MT bundles extending to the synapse from different sides (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Cited computational study and current ExM data showing centrosome trapping.

claim: In T cells, KIF21B acts at concentrations that are insufficient to induce prolonged pausing and effectively functions as a catastrophe inducer.
source: Therefore, we conclude that although biochemically KIF21B can be described as a MT pausing factor, in T cells, it acts at concentrations that are insufficient to induce prolonged pausing and effectively functions as a catastrophe inducer.
evidence: Integration of live-cell imaging data showing transient pausing followed by catastrophe.

claim: Blocking of even one MT protofilament by KIF21B can perturb growth of the remaining protofilaments and lead to loss of the GTP cap and trigger catastrophe.
source: This is likely explained by our previous observation that a single KIF21B-GFP molecule can arrest dynamics of a few protofilaments (van Riel et al., 2017). Blocking of even one MT protofilament can already perturb growth of the remaining ones, and this can lead to the loss of the GTP cap and trigger catastrophe (Doodhi et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited studies on protofilament dynamics and GTP cap loss mechanisms.

claim: KIF21B is a highly processive motor that would target longer MTs more effectively, similar to kinesin-8.
source: Furthermore, since KIF21B is a highly processive motor, it can be expected that it would target longer MTs more effectively, like it has been previously shown for kinesin-8 (Gupta et al., 2006; Varga et al., 2006).
evidence: Cited studies on kinesin-8 length-dependent targeting and inference about KIF21B behavior.

claim: The finding that KIF21B acts as an inhibitor of MT growth is in agreement with studies in neurons showing that KIF21B reduces MT growth processivity.
source: The finding that KIF21B acts as an inhibitor of MT growth is in agreement with the studies in neurons, which showed that KIF21B reduces MT growth processivity (Ghiretti et al., 2016; Muhia et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited neuronal studies consistent with current findings on KIF21B function.

claim: The immunological synapse facilitates T-cell signaling and polarized secretion of cytokines or lytic molecules toward the APC.
source: The immunological synapse facilitates T-cell signaling and polarized secretion of cytokines or lytic molecules toward the APC (Figure 1A).
evidence: Established knowledge about immunological synapse function.

claim: During T cell activation, lysosomes cluster around the centrosome and relocate together with it toward the synapse.
source: During T cell activation, lysosomes cluster around the centrosome and relocate together with it toward the synapse (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Established knowledge about lysosome behavior during T cell activation.

claim: Exposure to poly-D-lysine-coated coverslips did not trigger centrosome polarization or lysosome clustering in Jurkat cells.
source: We note that although it has been reported that cationic surfaces are sufficient to initiate T cell signaling (Santos et al., 2018), in our hands, exposure to poly-D-lysine-coated coverslips did not trigger centrosome polarization or lysosome clustering (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2H,I).
evidence: Experimental observation comparing poly-D-lysine to anti-CD3 activation.

claim: The centrosome needs to pass the nucleus along one side to move to the synapse when the nucleus is located between the centrosome and the synapse.
source: In cells where the nucleus is located between the centrosome and the synapse, as would often be the case in T cells migrating toward a chemoattractant (Roig-Martinez et al., 2019), the centrosome needs to pass it along one side to move to the synapse.
evidence: Geometric constraint inferred from cell structure and cited study on T cell migration.

claim: Asymmetric organization of MTs reaching the synapse from different sides of the nucleus likely originates from fluctuations in the number of MTs contacting the synapse.
source: This movement would require a force only on one side and thus an asymmetric organization of MTs reaching the synapse from the different sides of the nucleus. Such asymmetries likely originate from fluctuations in the number of MTs contacting the synapse from different sides that occur more readily when the number of MTs is low.
evidence: Inference from simulation results showing relationship between MT number and force asymmetry.

claim: Overly long MTs could slow down centrosome translocation by directly affecting dynein-mediated force generation.
source: Excessively long MTs could slow down centrosome translocation by directly affecting dynein-mediated force generation, for example, by reducing the number of MT ends contacting the synapse and perturbing MT end capture by dynein.
evidence: Speculation about additional mechanisms by which long MTs could impair polarization.

claim: Long MTs could make MT depolymerization-driven 'reeling in' of the centrosome less efficient or create pushing forces and friction that would inhibit repositioning of the MT network.
source: Long MTs could also make MT depolymerization-driven 'reeling in' of the centrosome less efficient or create pushing forces and friction that would inhibit repositioning of the MT network.
evidence: Speculation about mechanical effects of long MTs on centrosome movement.

claim: The presence of circular MT bundles might perturb synapse formation by affecting signaling-based cross-talk between MTs and actin.
source: We further note that even in cells that did relocate their centrosome, the immunological synapses formed slower and were smaller, suggesting that the presence of circular MT bundles might perturb synapse formation in some additional ways, for example, by affecting signaling-based cross-talk between MTs and actin (Dogterom and Koenderink, 2019).
evidence: Speculation about additional effects of MT bundles on synapse formation with cited reference.

claim: The typical features of MT network organization in T cells, with relatively short and sparse MTs, is functionally important.
source: Taken together, our data show that the typical features of MT network organization in T cells, with relatively short and sparse MTs, is functionally important and that its maintenance depends on a dedicated regulatory factor, KIF21B, which restricts MT growth.
evidence: Summary conclusion integrating all experimental and computational findings.
